ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
A bounded uniform magnetic field with a width of \( d \) and a magnetic induction intensity of \( B \), where \( MM^{\prime} \) and \( NN^{\prime} \) are its two boundaries. A charged particle with mass \( m \) and charge \( q \) is injected into the magnetic field perpendicularly along the direction shown in the diagram.

1. What could be the maximum value of the particle's incident velocity \( v \) to prevent the particle from escaping through the boundary \( NN^{\prime} \)?
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text: $(2+\sqrt{2})\frac{B q d}{m}$ (q is a positive charge) or $(2-\sqrt{2})\frac{B q d}{m}$ (q is a negative charge)

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, the magnetic-field region is a vertical narrow strip, the left boundary is labeled MM′, the right boundary is labeled NN′, and the spacing between the two boundaries is marked as d at the top. Many crosses are drawn inside the strip, indicating that the magnetic induction intensity B is perpendicular to the plane of the paper inward. The particle enters obliquely from the left boundary MM′ as shown in the figure, and the dashed line connects from the left-side point O to the incident position and gives a 45° geometric relationship. The figure also draws the circular-arc trajectory of the particle inside the magnetic field; the critical case corresponds to the rightmost end of the trajectory being just tangent to the right boundary NN′. Reasoning: After the particle enters the uniform magnetic field, it undergoes uniform circular motion, with radius R = mv/(|q|B). Take the left boundary where the incident point is located as x = 0, and the right boundary NN′ as x = d. Since the incident direction shown in the figure corresponds to 45°, the magnitude of the horizontal displacement of the center of the circle relative to the incident point is R/√2. When the trajectory just does not exit from NN′, the rightmost end of the circle satisfies x = d. When q is a positive charge and B is perpendicular to the plane of the paper inward, by the right-hand rule, the center of the circle is on the left side of the incident point, so the x-coordinate of the center is -R/√2, and the rightmost end of the circle is R - R/√2 = R(1 - 1/√2). Let d = R(1 - 1/√2), obtaining R = d/(1 - 1/√2) = (2 + √2)d, so v_max = |q|BR/m = (2 + √2)Bqd/m. When q is a negative charge, the center of the circle is on the opposite side, the x-coordinate of the center is +R/√2, and the rightmost end of the circle is R + R/√2 = R(1 + 1/√2). Let d = R(1 + 1/√2), obtaining R = d/(1 + 1/√2) = (2 - √2)d, so v_max = (2 - √2)B|q|d/m. If according to the problem solution q denotes the magnitude of the charge of the negative charge, then it is written as (2 - √2)Bqd/m.

A charged particle with mass \( m \) and charge \( q \) is injected into the magnetic field perpendicularly along the direction shown in the diagram.

method.method_draft: First describe the diagram: the magnetic field region is the vertical strip between the left boundary MM′ and the right boundary NN′, with horizontal width d; the crosses show B is directed into the page; the incident velocity shown at the left boundary makes a 45° direction relative to the horizontal/vertical construction indicated by the dashed line from O. Treat the motion in the field as uniform circular motion with radius R = mv/(|q|B). Put the entry point on MM′ at x = 0 and NN′ at x = d. Use the right-hand rule with B into the page to decide on which side of the initial velocity the circle center lies for q > 0 and q < 0. From the 45° incidence, the center’s horizontal coordinate differs from the entry point by R/√2. The orbit just fails to escape through NN′ when its farthest right point is tangent to x = d. Thus impose d = R(1 - 1/√2) for the charge sign whose center is to the left of the entry point, and d = R(1 + 1/√2) for the opposite sign. Then convert R back to v using v = |q|BR/m, giving the two possible maximum speeds: for positive q, v_max = (2 + √2)Bqd/m; for negative q, v_max = (2 - √2)Bqd/m, using the sign convention stated in the answer.
method.CoT_raw:
图像描述：图中磁场区域是竖直狭长条带，左边界标为 MM′，右边界标为 NN′，顶部标出两边界间距为 d。条带内画有许多叉号，表示磁感应强度 B 垂直纸面向里。粒子从左边界 MM′ 按图示斜向射入，虚线从左侧点 O 连到入射位置并给出 45° 几何关系。图中还画出了粒子在磁场内的圆弧轨迹，临界情形对应轨迹最右端刚好与右边界 NN′ 相切。

推理：粒子进入匀强磁场后做匀速圆周运动，半径为 R = mv/(|q|B)。取入射点所在左边界为 x = 0，右边界 NN′ 为 x = d。由于图示入射方向对应 45°，圆心相对入射点的水平位移大小为 R/√2。轨迹刚好不从 NN′ 射出时，圆周的最右端满足 x = d。

当 q 为正电荷且 B 垂直纸面向里时，由右手定则，圆心在入射点左侧，故圆心横坐标为 -R/√2，圆周最右端为 R - R/√2 = R(1 - 1/√2)。令 d = R(1 - 1/√2)，得 R = d/(1 - 1/√2) = (2 + √2)d，所以 v_max = |q|BR/m = (2 + √2)Bqd/m。

当 q 为负电荷时，圆心在相反一侧，圆心横坐标为 +R/√2，圆周最右端为 R + R/√2 = R(1 + 1/√2)。令 d = R(1 + 1/√2)，得 R = d/(1 + 1/√2) = (2 - √2)d，所以 v_max = (2 - √2)B|q|d/m。若按题解中 q 表示负电荷的电荷量大小，则写作 (2 - √2)Bqd/m。

method.method_draft: Use a purely geometric limiting-orbit construction. From the diagram, identify that the largest allowed velocity corresponds to the circular trajectory that only grazes NN′; if the radius were any larger, the arc would cross the right boundary. Draw the circle center Q on the normal to the incident velocity at the entry point. Because the velocity direction shown is at 45°, the line from the entry point to Q also has 45° components, so the horizontal projection from the entry point to Q is R/√2. The rightmost point of the circular orbit lies another distance R horizontally from Q. Depending on the sign of q, the Lorentz force places Q on the side that either reduces or increases the distance from MM′ to the orbit’s rightmost point. Therefore the grazing condition gives d = R - R/√2 for the positive-charge case shown by the larger-radius arc, and d = R + R/√2 for the negative-charge case shown by the smaller-radius arc. Solve these as R = (2 + √2)d or R = (2 - √2)d respectively, then substitute R = mv/(|q|B) to obtain v_max = (2 + √2)Bqd/m for q > 0 and v_max = (2 - √2)Bqd/m for q < 0.

raw_record.original_question:
A bounded uniform magnetic field with a width of \( d \) and a magnetic induction intensity of \( B \), where \( MM^{\prime} \) and \( NN^{\prime} \) are its two boundaries. A charged particle with mass \( m \) and charge \( q \) is injected into the magnetic field perpendicularly along the direction shown in the diagram.

1. What could be the maximum value of the particle's incident velocity \( v \) to prevent the particle from escaping through the boundary \( NN^{\prime} \)?
raw_record.answer: $(2+\sqrt{2})\frac{B q d}{m}$ (q is a positive charge) or $(2-\sqrt{2})\frac{B q d}{m}$ (q is a negative charge)
raw_record.final_cot:
Image description: In the figure, the magnetic-field region is a vertical narrow strip, the left boundary is labeled MM′, the right boundary is labeled NN′, and the spacing between the two boundaries is marked as d at the top. Many crosses are drawn inside the strip, indicating that the magnetic induction intensity B is perpendicular to the plane of the paper inward. The particle enters obliquely from the left boundary MM′ as shown in the figure, and the dashed line connects from the left-side point O to the incident position and gives a 45° geometric relationship. The figure also draws the circular-arc trajectory of the particle inside the magnetic field; the critical case corresponds to the rightmost end of the trajectory being just tangent to the right boundary NN′.

Reasoning: After the particle enters the uniform magnetic field, it undergoes uniform circular motion, with radius R = mv/(|q|B). Take the left boundary where the incident point is located as x = 0, and the right boundary NN′ as x = d. Since the incident direction shown in the figure corresponds to 45°, the magnitude of the horizontal displacement of the center of the circle relative to the incident point is R/√2. When the trajectory just does not exit from NN′, the rightmost end of the circle satisfies x = d.

When q is a positive charge and B is perpendicular to the plane of the paper inward, by the right-hand rule, the center of the circle is on the left side of the incident point, so the x-coordinate of the center is -R/√2, and the rightmost end of the circle is R - R/√2 = R(1 - 1/√2). Let d = R(1 - 1/√2), obtaining R = d/(1 - 1/√2) = (2 + √2)d, so v_max = |q|BR/m = (2 + √2)Bqd/m.

When q is a negative charge, the center of the circle is on the opposite side, the x-coordinate of the center is +R/√2, and the rightmost end of the circle is R + R/√2 = R(1 + 1/√2). Let d = R(1 + 1/√2), obtaining R = d/(1 + 1/√2) = (2 - √2)d, so v_max = (2 - √2)B|q|d/m. If according to the problem solution q denotes the magnitude of the charge of the negative charge, then it is written as (2 - √2)Bqd/m.
